name: Ivan Evans

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I’m with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What does an ordinary workday look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am 58 and principal oboe, meaning I lead the oboe section of our regional orchestra and play its opening solos. I also record exam passages and coach two pupils. My music master’s helps at the stand, though the written season contract matters just as much at home.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What part of that day do you like, and what takes the energy out of it?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I like hearing a young player settle an entrance after a difficult rehearsal. The orchestra pays a normal rate and my partner earns a museum wage, so we have four months saved. I dislike contracts that pay once for a recording and say nothing about later copies; I do not use AI tools myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I lead the oboes at the regional orchestra, and the exam publishers still book my recorded passages. In AI Plateau I would tell our section this: A faster booking email does not play my oboe's opening solo. I would keep the signed season and the two pupils I coach after rehearsals.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The orchestra contract and my partner's museum wage are steady, and we have four months of expenses put away. I have watched enough budgets to know that one season is not a lifetime, but one missed recording invoice would not break us now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I will keep the signed rehearsals and pupil sessions, then put ten percent of each paid exam-recording fee into the reserve after bills clear. I will do the same in the first year of a mild AI change until the reserve reaches six months of expenses. I will ask the orchestra for its next season's written dates at the usual renewal meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be calm about a small software change. I would still watch the renewal letter, as any section leader should.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does your four-month reserve let you do?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It lets me wait for the proper fee instead of saying yes to an unpaid recording. It would not support us forever if the orchestra chair disappeared.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you use the new booking software yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used an AI tool and do not need to start for a booking email. Our administrator can send the dates, and I will check the written call sheet as I always do.

say: A **booking shortcut** will not play the oboe solo in our signed orchestra season.
I would tell the section to check the **written call sheet** before changing rehearsals.
think: The **orchestra contract** and museum wage cover current bills, with four months saved.
A **missed recording fee** is manageable today, though the next season still matters.
do: Keep **signed rehearsals** and two pupil sessions through the first mild-change year.
Save **ten percent** of each cleared exam-recording fee after bills until six months are reserved.
Request **written next-season dates** at the usual orchestra renewal meeting.
feel: I feel **calm** about small automation while I monitor the contract renewal.
fieldNote: His **calm** rests on booked work, a partner wage, and a four-month reserve.
He **declines AI tools** and checks written call sheets himself, consistent with his familiar routine.
S0.quote: A faster booking email does not play my oboe's opening solo.

steps.text: Keep signed orchestra rehearsals and two pupil sessions
Save ten percent of cleared exam-recording fees after bills toward six months
Request written next-season dates at orchestra renewal

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the section that Steady Disruption can draft exam passages and concert notes, but a publisher must still pay for a musician's recording or get permission to reuse it. I do not want my pupils' takes fed into a system without their consent. At the union meeting I would ask for a written reuse fee, not a vague promise about exposure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Exam passages are about a fifth of my pay, and those buyers may shrink before the orchestra loses a chair. The four-month reserve gives me time to speak up, but I do not want to spend it replacing a regular invoice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I will take our publisher contracts to the musicians' union and ask it to bargain for recording consent and a per-use fee. I will keep the signed orchestra and pupil work. In the first disruption year I will accept new recorded work only with written pay and reuse limits, and I will keep putting ten percent of cleared recording fees after household bills into the reserve while they exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about the recording fifth, though I can still rehearse and negotiate. A good solo will not stop a publisher from buying a cheaper file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring to the union meeting?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would bring the two contracts that pay once but say nothing about copying the recording later. Names of my pupils would stay off the papers I share.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a publisher says the fee covers all future uses?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the union to put a price and time limit on reuse before signing another session. If the publisher will not write it down, I keep the orchestra call and decline that recording.

say: A publisher should pay for **recording reuse** and obtain consent before making copies.
I would bring the **written contracts** to the union rather than share pupil recordings.
think: My **exam-recording fifth** could lose buyers while the live orchestra chair remains.
Four months of **reserve** buys time to negotiate, not a lasting replacement income.
do: Bring **publisher contracts** to the union this month and request consent, limits, and per-use fees.
Keep **signed work** in the orchestra and with pupils during the first disruption year.
Accept new **recorded sessions** only with written pay and reuse limits; save ten percent of cleared fees.
feel: I feel **anxious** about the recording share but able to negotiate and keep playing.
fieldNote: His **union request** concerns specific contracts, consent, and per-use pay rather than a general slogan.
He expects **recording losses**, with the orchestra chair continuing for now.
S1.quote: A good solo will not stop a publisher from buying a cheaper file.

steps.text: Bring publisher contracts to union; request written consent, limits, and per-use fees
Keep signed orchestra and pupil work in first disruption year
Save ten percent of cleared recording fees after household bills

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my section that AGI by 2028 could erase the exam-recording orders before a robot plays beside us around 2031. I would ask the union to publish the actual recording fees lost, so the orchestra knows what is at stake. I would still turn up for every paid rehearsal on the signed calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the recording fifth of my own pay to end in 2028. Four months saved and my partner's museum wage give us some control, but neither becomes a fifth of my earnings every year. A later cut to orchestra calls would be worse; I am not treating that as certain now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will request an actual pension estimate this month and keep all signed orchestra and pupil calls. If exam orders end in 2028, I will audition only for a posted paid principal-oboe opening that accepts my music master's and a live audition. In the first year after AGI I will stay in my current paid chair until a signed offer gives written take-home pay after travel that replaces the lost recording fifth, with transport I can actually use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious, not helpless. The recording loss is likely in this picture, but I have some savings, a partner wage, and a paid chair while I search.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why request a pension estimate instead of naming a retirement age?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 60, I need the actual figure to know how much playing we still require at 68. A four-month reserve is not a pension, and I cannot assume a payment I have not checked.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you take a better orchestra chair before an offer is signed?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I will audition while employed, but I cannot give up the current section for a hopeful conversation. The new orchestra must put the pay after travel, the dates, and the offer in writing first.

say: The **exam recordings** could end in 2028, while playing robots arrive around 2031.
I would ask the union to document **lost recording fees** using actual contracts.
think: I expect a **fifth of my pay** from recordings to end quickly.
Our **four-month reserve** and museum wage soften the loss without replacing it year after year.
do: Request an **actual pension estimate** and keep signed orchestra and pupil calls this month.
Audition after **exam orders end** only for posted principal-oboe work accepting my master's and live audition.
Keep current chair until **signed net pay** after travel replaces lost fees and usable transport is confirmed.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a likely recording loss, with savings and a paid chair giving me options.
fieldNote: The **recording loss** is expected; a later orchestra cut remains conditional and does not drive his mood.
The **audition** is conditional on a posted qualifying opening, signed replacement net pay, and workable travel.
S2.quote: A four-month reserve is not a pension, and I cannot assume a payment I have not checked.

steps.text: Request actual pension estimate and keep signed orchestra and pupil calls
Audition after exam orders end for posted principal-oboe role accepting master’s and live audition
Keep current chair until signed net pay after travel replaces fees and transport works

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell our union members that AGI by 2031 gives us five years to write a fair recording clause before buyers change, while playing robots follow around 2034. I would bring a proposed minimum rehearsal fee and a separate reuse price to the next bargaining round. My oboe chair is paid live work, not permission for free studio copies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The extra years help, but publishers may stop buying my exam passages before 2031 anyway. I make my own reeds, the small cane mouthpieces that vibrate when I play, and a paid preorder for those could be another source. I would not carve a box of oboe reeds for compliments and hope someone pays later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I will price ten custom reed orders, including cane, postage, my cutting time, and safe packaging, and ask buyers for payment before I make them. I will make them outside paid orchestra calls and refund any order I cannot deliver safely. In the first year after 2031 I will continue only if repeat paid orders cover the same full costs, keep the signed chair, and request the actual pension estimate instead of guessing when I can stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about exam work, but I can test ten real orders without risking the orchestra cheque. The five years are useful only if I use them while the contract still pays.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you sell reeds to your pupils?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Only if a pupil asks and has the right instrument; lessons will not become a sales pitch. I would also tell them another maker can fit a reed better than I can for their mouth.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a failed preorder test?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If the ten deposits do not cover cane, postage, cutting time, and safe packing, the price is wrong. I would return the payments rather than use our household reserve to subsidise orders.

say: I would bargain for a **separate reuse fee** and a paid rehearsal minimum before 2031.
I would offer **custom oboe reeds** only as prepaid work outside orchestra calls.
think: The **exam buyers** may leave before 2031 despite five years of warning.
Ten **paid reed orders** could test a separate income source without spending the household reserve.
do: Bring **reuse fee terms** and rehearsal pay to the next union bargaining round.
Take **ten reed preorders** only when full costs are paid; refund orders that cannot be delivered safely.
Keep **orchestra calls** and request actual pension estimate; continue reed orders after 2031 only at full cost.
feel: I feel **anxious** about exam buyers, with time for paid bargaining and a small preorder test.
fieldNote: The **reed preorders** are separate maker income grounded in his own oboe craft and paid before production.
He keeps **current paid calls** and seeks a pension estimate rather than assuming retirement is affordable.
S3.quote: I would not carve a box of oboe reeds for compliments and hope someone pays later.

steps.text: Bring reuse and rehearsal fee terms to next union bargaining round
Take ten reed preorders only if payment covers cane, postage, cutting time, and safe packing
Refund unsafe or uneconomic reed orders; renew after 2031 only at full cost
Keep orchestra calls and request actual pension estimate

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell the section that AGI by 2036 offers a decade to defend paid recordings, while stage robots are later, around 2039. We should write rehearsal, recording, and reuse fees into each agreement now. I would still play the oboe at 68 if the chair is paid and my hands permit it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The long warning is helpful, but it does not guarantee an orchestra seat for another decade. Exam publishers may buy less before 2036, and our present four-month reserve will not tell me what a pension pays. My grown children have their own lives; I do not count their income as mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I will request my actual pension estimate, keep signed orchestra and pupil work, and put ten percent of cleared recording fees toward a six-month reserve after bills. I will bring written reuse terms to the union’s next renewal meeting. In the first year after 2036, if recorded pay falls, I will audition for a posted paid principal-oboe opening with human rehearsal duties only if my master’s and experience qualify. I will keep my current paid chair until a signed offer gives written take-home pay after travel replacing lost fees and usable transport.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am anxious about the publishers, though a decade gives us time to negotiate. Retirement has to be a number on a statement, not a birthday on a calendar.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire when stage robots become capable in 2039?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I might still have a paid chair at 71, or I might prefer fewer calls, but I cannot name that decision today. The pension statement, my health, and actual fees will decide more than the robot date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens if a posted role pays less after travel?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not resign for a grand title that leaves less in our account. I would keep the current paid work and look at the next real opening rather than borrow against an uncertain pension.

say: We should put **rehearsal and recording fees** into written agreements during the decade.
I would keep a paid **human oboe chair** while stage robots remain a later question.
think: The **exam market** may weaken before 2036 even with more warning.
An **unknown pension** and four-month reserve do not prove that retirement is funded.
do: Request **actual pension estimate**, keep signed orchestra and pupil work until a replacement offer, and bring reuse terms to union renewal.
Save **ten percent** of cleared recording fees after bills toward six months of expenses.
Audition after **recording loss** for posted paid human-led principal-oboe work accepting my master’s; require signed replacement net after travel and usable transport.
feel: I feel **anxious** about declining exam fees while the decade leaves time to negotiate.
fieldNote: He **does not assume retirement** at 68 or robot arrival; the pension estimate and current fees matter.
The **possible new role** needs a posted human-led vacancy, accepted qualifications, signed replacement net pay, and transport.
S4.quote: Retirement has to be a number on a statement, not a birthday on a calendar.

steps.text: Request pension estimate; keep signed orchestra and pupil work until a replacement offer
Save ten percent of cleared recording fees after bills toward six months
Bring written reuse terms to union renewal meeting
Audition after recording loss for posted principal-oboe role; require master’s, signed replacement net-after-travel pay, usable buses

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because the recording fifth could disappear quickly, with no time to bargain. A signed principal-oboe opening with qualifying terms, written replacement pay after travel, and an actual pension estimate would let me plan. The union could also secure consent and reuse fees before publishers change their contracts.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who owns the first clean recording after the musician goes home. A publisher can keep selling my old oboe take while I wait for the next paid call.

headlineQuote: A publisher can keep selling my old oboe take while I wait for the next paid call.
portrait: Ivan is a **58-year-old** principal oboist with a music master’s, recording exam passages and coaching two pupils.
His orchestra contract, partner’s museum wage, and **four-month reserve** support current bills.
He avoids **AI tools** and asks his union for written recording consent and reuse pay.
He tests **prepaid reeds** as separate maker income while keeping the signed orchestra chair.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his recording fifth before a new contract or job is secured.
whatWouldHelp: A qualifying **principal-oboe vacancy**, signed replacement net pay after travel, pension estimate, and union reuse terms would help.
